problem: US DOT publishes every flight's on-time record as about 6.5 million rows a year with 109 columns. Travellers and operators want four plain answers: which airports, which airlines, which hours, and why.
contribution: Solo project. I built the star schema (635,459 flights, four dimensions), the DAX measures with a whole-Florida benchmark, the report in Power BI Service, and a pandas script that recomputes every card to test it.
result: 75.5% on time; time of day matters about twice as much as the airline, and late-arriving aircraft cause 42.5% of delay minutes. The interactive version on this site is a web preview of the same model.

problem: Raw sales exports are never analysis-ready: duplicate rows, postage mixed with products, cancellations hiding inside sales. Every analyst cleans the file again, differently.
contribution: Solo project. I wrote the staging, intermediate and mart layers in dbt on DuckDB over 1.07 million invoice lines, a seed of business rules, 31 data tests (five written for this data) and the generated lineage docs.
result: Net sales £18.18M after £1.46M of cancellations; champions are 25.1% of customers and 70.8% of revenue. Runs on demand on a laptop, no scheduler or warehouse.

problem: Chicago's Divvy bike-share has annual members and casual riders. How do they use the bikes differently, and where would a membership campaign reach the most casual riders?
contribution: Solo project. I loaded 6.1 million trips into SQLite, wrote one SQL file per question (CTEs, window functions, indexes), and a plain-Python recount that must agree exactly with every SQL answer.
result: Members ride 65% of trips and commute at 8:00 and 17:00; casual riders own the lakefront on summer weekends (Navy Pier: 75.9% casual). The campaign recommendation follows from the patterns, not a tested result.

problem: Monthly US retail sales swing hard with the calendar. A forecast has to get the seasonal shape right, and it is only worth something if you know how wrong it tends to be.
contribution: Solo project. I built the pipeline on Census data from 1992 onward: seasonal indices, five methods, a rolling-origin backtest, and ranges calibrated on the backtest's real errors.
result: The ETS + SARIMA average scored 1.81% MAPE, 35% smaller errors than 'same month last year'. The calibrated 80% range is about 40% narrower than the models' own.

problem: Market research starts with 'how many businesses of each kind are in this city, and where?' Paid lead databases answer it but hide how they count.
contribution: Solo project. I built the ETL pipeline from GeoNames, US Census ZIP areas and OpenStreetMap into SQLite, the rule-based active / unknown / likely-closed label, and a FastAPI app with a table, dashboard and map.
result: Tampa, FL: 6,298 businesses after cleaning, 5,425 inside city limits. 60% are labelled unknown on purpose: most small businesses carry no evidence either way.

problem: A source quietly changes what it sends. Every job still finishes green, and the revenue dashboard is wrong. Can software notice the same morning, say what else is affected, and point to where it started?
contribution: Solo project from a written blueprint. I built the Python and PostgreSQL service: lineage discovery (72 assets, 82 links), daily profiles, anomaly detection against each table's own history, incident grouping and root-cause ranking, with 34 tests.
result: Across 108 planted failures the true origin ranked first 94% of the time, against 31% for blaming the loudest alert. The warehouse is simulated, so every result is checked against a known answer.

problem: A 10-K runs to hundreds of pages. A chatbot answers fluently, but a fluent wrong number is worse than no answer. Can an LLM answer only from the filings, cite the passage, and admit when the answer is not there?
contribution: Solo project. I parsed five companies' latest 10-Ks from SEC EDGAR into 730 passages, compared keyword, embedding and hybrid search, and graded 30 questions against XBRL figures.
result: 20/20 money answers within 0.5% of XBRL with the figure in the cited passage, 5/5 correct refusals, $0.10 for all 30. The demo shows recorded answers; this site never calls an API.

problem: Excel is still where most financial analysis happens, and a model is only as good as how it is built: inputs apart from formulas, scenarios that switch, checks that catch mistakes.
contribution: Solo project. I built the six-sheet Costco workbook from SEC XBRL history: scenario switch, driver-based forecast to FY2030, DCF with a 5 × 5 sensitivity grid, and six self-checks.
result: 231 live formulas; the base case runs from $194 to $399 a share across the grid, so the grid is the result to read. A modelling exercise, not investment advice.
